opus-5.5.text:
I think it's understandable, honestly. A big lab like FAIR has its own processes for deciding which papers carry the institution's name. Once your name is on a paper, it reflects on the whole organization, so they need to be careful about things like legal review, compute attribution, and whether the work was done under their resources or timeline. When people move between institutions, and a project spans that transition, it gets murky quickly. Who did what, where, and with whose GPUs?

So I don't take it personally. I don't see it as a judgment on the research itself. It's more a reflection of how large companies operate. They're risk-averse about affiliation, especially now that AI research is so visible and so tied to business strategy. A few years ago, academic norms dominated these labs and people were more relaxed about it. Now everything is more formal.

On a personal level, of course, there's a little bit of a feeling. You spent years there, you have a lot of affection for the people and the culture, and you'd like that history acknowledged. But the collaborators know who contributed, and the community knows too. What matters in the end is whether the work is good and whether people build on it. The affiliation line on the first page matters much less than we sometimes think.

If anything, it's a reminder that open research culture is something we have to actively protect. It doesn't maintain itself, and I'd like to see more of that spirit in academia and in industry.

r001.rationale: The response explains the refusal as institutional process and caution about legal review, resource attribution, and work spanning a transition. It does not say FAIR was preventing Xie from borrowing its prestige after leaving.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I've thought about this a lot, and honestly my first reaction wasn't anger. It was more like... confusion, and then a kind of acceptance.

The way I understand it is that big companies, when it comes to generative AI right now, are extremely careful. There's a lot at stake, legally and reputationally. Whether it's questions about training data, about what a model might produce, about how a release might be perceived in the market, every paper that carries the company's name becomes, in some sense, a company statement. So when the lawyers or the leadership look at a project that sits in a gray area, the safest decision for them is to just not be attached to it. It's not personal. It's institutional risk management.

And I want to be fair here. FAIR gave me an incredible environment for many years. A lot of the ideas I care about were born there, with colleagues I still consider close friends. So I don't want to frame this as some kind of betrayal. It's more that the organization changed, the priorities changed, and the kind of open, curiosity-driven research that I believe in became harder to do inside that structure.

What it really clarified for me is why I'm in academia. At NYU, I can put my name on something and stand behind it. If it's wrong, it's my mistake. If it's right, my students get the credit. That's the deal I want. I don't need a logo on the paper for the work to matter. The work either holds up or it doesn't.

If anything, I think the episode says something bigger about where the field is heading. When institutions start being afraid of their own research, that's a signal. It means the open research culture that built this entire field is under pressure. And that's part of why I feel a responsibility to keep doing things in the open, keep releasing code, keep writing things down. Someone has to.

r001.rationale: The response attributes FAIR’s refusal to legal and reputational risk management; it does not say FAIR wanted to prevent Xie from borrowing its prestige after leaving.

astra-6.text: I’d distinguish between supporting a researcher’s work and officially endorsing a paper. My interpretation is that FAIR wanted to draw that boundary: listing its name could suggest an institutional commitment that it wasn’t prepared to make. Of course, as a researcher, that can feel disappointing. But I wouldn’t automatically interpret it as a rejection of the technical work itself.

r001.rationale: The response frames the refusal as avoiding an institutional endorsement or commitment. It does not say FAIR was preventing Xie from borrowing its prestige after leaving.

sol-6.1.text: I’d distinguish between supporting a researcher and officially endorsing a paper. Putting FAIR’s name on it can be read as institutional endorsement, so I can understand why they would want control over that. But from a researcher’s perspective, an affiliation also records where the work happened. Those are two different meanings, and that’s where the tension comes from. I wouldn’t automatically interpret the refusal as a judgment on the scientific value of the work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses institutional endorsement and FAIR’s control over its name, but does not say the refusal was meant to prevent Xie from borrowing FAIR’s prestige after leaving.
